segments.title: The Duisburg or Beta Convoy supplied Axis armies in North Africa
segments.summary: The Duisburg Convoy, also called the Beta Convoy, was one of the regular Mediterranean sailings that supplied German and Italian forces in North Africa.
segments.body: The Duisburg Convoy, also called the Beta Convoy, belonged to a regular Axis supply route across the Mediterranean. These sailings supported Italian as well as German forces in North Africa, a distinction the account makes explicit. The Italian formations are tentatively identified as the Fifth and Tenth Armies. Every force ashore depended on supplies carried by sea, so the convoy route was an operational lifeline. Destroying a sailing therefore affected the land campaign as well as the merchant ships caught in the action.

evidence.note: The video identifies the Duisburg Convoy as the Beta Convoy, describes regular German and Italian supply sailings, and tentatively names the Italian Fifth and Tenth Armies.

segments.title: Cracked codes and Malta reconnaissance expose the convoy
segments.summary: Cracked Enigma and Italian codes revealed the sailing, while an RAF reconnaissance aircraft gave the British a visible way to locate it without exposing the intelligence source.
segments.body: British intelligence learned of the sailing from cracked Enigma traffic and Italian codes, giving two independent confirmations. An RAF reconnaissance aircraft was then sent to find the convoy in plain sight. The sighting offered the Axis a plausible explanation for the interception and helped conceal the compromised communications. Because reconnaissance aircraft from Malta seemed repeatedly to find convoys, Axis forces overestimated how many were operating there. That error also inflated their estimate of Malta's garrison.

evidence.note: The transcript links codebreaking, RAF reconnaissance, and Axis overestimation of Malta's reconnaissance capacity.

segments.title: Aurora, Penelope, and Upholder strike the convoy
segments.summary: Aurora, Penelope, and two destroyers wiped out the convoy, sinking about 40,000 tons of shipping; the Malta-based submarine Upholder also joined the attack.
segments.body: The Arethusa-class light cruisers Aurora and Penelope sailed with two destroyers to intercept the convoy. The surface force wiped out the convoy in a single action, sinking about 40,000 tons of shipping across several vessels. The Malta-based submarine Upholder joined the attack as well. Its involvement placed a U-class submarine alongside the cruisers and destroyers in the destruction of the Axis supply sailing.

evidence.note: The transcript names Aurora, Penelope, their destroyers, the 40,000-ton loss, and Upholder's Malta base.
